claim: Across three code-interaction modalities, the strongest LLM judges underperform human majority agreement by 12-23 percentage points, and no single judge model dominates across modalities.
stance_target: reliability of LLM-based rubric/partial-credit judging as a ground truth for code evaluation
scope_conditions: 13 LLM judges, chat-based programming, IDE autocompletion, instructed code editing; CMU study, 2026
quoted_support: the strongest judges among the evaluated models still underperformed aggregate human annotators... top judges trailing human agreement by 12-23% on every benchmark and no single model consistently dominating

claim: Fine-tuned specialized judge LLMs do not reliably outperform general-purpose third-party models as code evaluators, suggesting judge misalignment is not simply a specialization/training-data problem.
stance_target: limits of fine-tuning as a fix for code-evaluation judge quality
quoted_support: Notably, fine-tuned judge LLMs do not reliably outperform general-purpose models, suggesting that current shortcomings are not solely due to training data or specialization.

claim: Performance on established LLM-judge benchmarks (RewardBench, JudgeBench) correlates only weakly with judge accuracy on realistic developer-interaction code tasks, so external judge-benchmark scores do not reliably predict practical rubric/partial-credit evaluation quality.
stance_target: caution against relying on generic judge benchmarks to validate a code-evaluation methodology
scope_conditions: comparison of RewardBench/RewardBench2/JudgeBench-Coding scores vs TRACE modality accuracy
quoted_support: performance on our modalities aligns only weakly with established judge benchmarks... Strong results on external judge tasks do not necessarily carry over.
numbers: Skywork Critic: 93.3% RewardBench vs 32.0% CodeEdit accuracy
